what_it_does: A stable vitamin C derivative used as an antioxidant and skin-conditioning ingredient.
summary_short: Magnesium ascorbyl phosphate is a water-soluble vitamin C derivative valued for being more stable than pure ascorbic acid. It is used mainly as an antioxidant, though older skin-absorption research suggests it may not raise skin vitamin C levels as effectively as well-formulated L-ascorbic acid.
summary_long:
Magnesium ascorbyl phosphate, often shortened to MAP, is a derivative of vitamin C designed to be more stable and water-friendly than pure L-ascorbic acid. In cosmetics, it is used primarily as an antioxidant, meaning it helps protect formulas and skin from oxidative stress related to UV exposure and environmental damage [PMID:unknown].

Its main skincare appeal is that it offers a gentler, more stable way to include a vitamin C-related ingredient in a product. Pure L-ascorbic acid needs a low pH to enter skin well, which can make some formulas more irritating. In one percutaneous absorption study, L-ascorbic acid increased skin vitamin C levels only under specific formulation conditions, while magnesium ascorbyl phosphate did not increase measured L-ascorbic acid levels in skin in that model [PMID:unknown]. This means MAP should not be assumed to perform exactly like pure vitamin C.

The cosmetic safety review reported MAP use in products at about 0.001% to 3% and concluded that vitamin C and related ascorbate ingredients are safe as used in cosmetics [PMID:unknown]. MAP is generally positioned as a lower-irritation vitamin C option, though any active-containing product can still sting or irritate sensitive or compromised skin.

Evidence for MAP specifically in facial skincare is more limited than for L-ascorbic acid. Some non-cosmetic research suggests MAP can interact with collagen systems and wound-healing models, but those findings do not directly prove visible anti-aging or brightening benefits in everyday skincare products [PMID:unknown]. For consumers, the most practical takeaway is that MAP is a stable antioxidant ingredient, but results depend heavily on the overall formula.

MAP is commonly found in water-based serums, moisturizers, and antioxidant blends. It generally pairs well with hydrators, barrier-supporting ingredients, sunscreen, and other antioxidants. Formulators should avoid conditions that push ascorbate ingredients toward pro-oxidant behavior, especially problematic metal-ion interactions, which the safety review flagged as a formulation consideration [PMID:unknown].
quick_facts: Often gentler than pure vitamin C
Not the same as L-ascorbic acid
